title: Founders, Friction, and Focus: Building Engineering Teams at Early-Stage Startups
gist: David Gudeman, co-founder and CTO of Velocity AI, argues early-stage startup outcomes are disproportionately determined by founder personality quirks, that importing scrum from a big company at Actium made delivery predictable while destroying the velocity needed to find product-market fit (the company later sold for little), and that engineers should treat equity at seed/Series A as likely worth zero — citing friends at Figma whose stock price is in the gutter.

themes.theme: Founder personality as organizational risk factor

insights.claim: Early-stage startups are so dependent on founder personalities that small personality quirks balloon into major organizational issues — avoidant founders let existential issues fester, erratic founders thrash the team on whims, and excitement-seeking founders get bored precisely when something is working.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence taxonomy for seed investors: screen founder temperament on avoidance, erraticism and novelty-seeking, not just market and traction.
insights.quote: things that might be small personality quirks can then be ballooned into major organizational issues
insights.locator: How Founder Personalities Shape Organizations

insights.claim: People joining early-stage startups from stable corporate environments are routinely shocked at how much a single founder's behaviour defines their day-to-day experience, an effect far more pronounced than in a corporate setting.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Explains a hidden source of early-stage attrition that shows up as unexplained senior departures rather than as a stated culture problem.
insights.locator: How Founder Personalities Shape Organizations

insights.claim: Gudeman identifies unaddressed thrash at the top — leadership repeatedly promising new integrations and new verticals — as the biggest issue at Actium, and argues engineering's most valuable intervention would have been quantifying the runway cost of constant switching rather than improving its own predictability.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Strategic thrash burns capital faster than engineering inefficiency does; measure commitment churn at the leadership level as a burn-rate leading indicator.
insights.quote: If you keep promising this new type of integration when we have two or three already and you add a new vertical, you burn enormous amounts of resources for unclear advantage in the market
insights.locator: Finding the Right Amount of Process

insights.claim: After Actium hired someone from a much bigger company who imposed a top-down scrum process, predictability improved but velocity was destroyed — pre-scrum the team shipped more, with more bugs, but got product into users' hands much faster.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Process maturity imported from scale companies can be actively value-destroying pre-PMF; treat a new scrum rollout at an early-stage portfolio company as a risk event.
insights.quote: After the top-down imposition of this scrum process, the predictability became "better", but the velocity was destroyed.
insights.locator: The Danger of Predictability over Progress

insights.claim: Because most things a startup builds are not the right thing, the rate at which features can be tested and disqualified is the critical feedback loop that determines whether the startup as a whole succeeds — so doubling the time to run that loop is a strategic loss even if delivery quality improves.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Measure learning cycles per quarter, not ship predictability, when judging whether an early-stage team is progressing.
insights.quote: We're delivering product that has no bugs. It was delivered exactly the date that we specified, but we are ultimately not discovering product market fit quickly
insights.locator: The Danger of Predictability over Progress

insights.claim: Actium was ultimately acquired for not a lot, which Gudeman ties back to optimising for predictability rather than speed of product-market-fit discovery, calling the intervention the wrong move.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A worked example connecting a process decision to a weak exit outcome — the kind of causal chain worth probing in post-mortems of underperforming holdings.
insights.quote: And ultimately, the company got acquired for not a lot.
insights.locator: The Danger of Predictability over Progress

insights.claim: Gudeman rejects the premise that a process works universally and instead prescribes surveying the team's existing composition, identifying strengths, leaving what works untouched, and applying process narrowly to minimise specific weaknesses.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A targeted-intervention rule for operators: process should be prescribed against a diagnosed weakness, not installed wholesale.
insights.quote: The composition of the team really determines the process.
insights.locator: Finding the Right Amount of Process

insights.claim: Gudeman treats JIRA burndown charts and litigating ticket language as the visible symptom of lost trust, arguing that culture makes sense at 10,000 engineers but signals a startup has surrendered the adaptability that was supposed to be its competitive advantage.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: An observable diagnostic during company visits: adversarial ticket hygiene at small scale is a trust-failure indicator, not a maturity indicator.
insights.quote: the trust becomes so lost where you have JIRA burndown charts and it's like you're going over every ticket and then they become litigating the language in the ticket and it just becomes like a grudge match
insights.locator: What Makes a Team Great

insights.claim: Gudeman names being penny wise and pound foolish at the beginning — hiring excessively junior people too early without enough guidance — as one of the most critical mistakes he has seen, because those hires make architectural and technical decisions a more expensive experienced engineer would have avoided.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Early salary savings convert into architectural debt that compounds; scrutinise seniority mix in seed-stage engineering teams as a forward cost.
insights.quote: you hire excessively junior people too early and there's not enough guidance
insights.locator: Growing a Well-Crafted Engineering Team From Nothing

insights.claim: Founders who view the engineering team as a cost center rather than an asset to invest in are making the framing error that leads to under-hiring at the start.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: How a founder describes engineering spend in a pitch is a cheap signal of whether the team will be built as an asset or a line item.
insights.quote: they view it as a cost center as opposed to an investment
insights.locator: Growing a Well-Crafted Engineering Team From Nothing

insights.claim: A well-functioning early-stage team shows alignment at every level plus trust at every level, delivers on the appropriate — not maximum — level of quality negotiated among stakeholders, and writes down only what is needed to make institutional knowledge permanent rather than as an adversarial measuring stick.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A checklist for assessing early-stage engineering health without access to metrics dashboards.
insights.locator: What Makes a Team Great

insights.claim: As Actium's team grew it fragmented into tribes — data people with a different stack and cadence interfacing with customer success, and product engineers answering to the product team — that remained heavily interdependent, and the attempted fix was applied overzealously.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Scaling failures usually appear first as stack and cadence divergence between interdependent sub-teams — an early warning to watch during headcount ramps.
insights.locator: Navigating Team Growth and Re-Teaming

insights.claim: Gudeman argues influence must be pre-built: if you have not cultivated relationships with stakeholders and given them evidence to invest in your opinion before the bad decision arrives, you have already lost at the moment it lands.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Relationship capital is a lagging-to-build asset; leaders should be judged on whether they invested in it before a crisis, not during one.
insights.quote: If you haven't developed a relationship with the stakeholders and provided them evidence why they should invest in your opinion, when that moment comes, you've kind of already lost
insights.locator: Influencing Without Positional Power

insights.claim: Engineers become persuasive by staying engaged with the people who face customers directly and bringing their stories into the conversation, rather than by arguing in technical implementation language which gets consumed confusingly if at all.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A concrete behavioural marker distinguishing engineers who will scale into leadership from those who will stall.
insights.locator: Influencing Without Positional Power

insights.claim: Gudeman moved into product specifically because he judged product to be the place to influence misguided decisions, but found product at that organization was treated as an order taker rather than a driver of strategy and vision.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Whether product functions as order taker or strategy driver is a structural determinant of whether an org can course-correct.
insights.locator: Influencing Without Positional Power

insights.claim: Some leaders cannot tolerate resistance in public forums but are open to it one-on-one, so floating an unpointed criticism in a public setting lets it be absorbed by the group and socialised among the decision maker's peers.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A tactical routing rule for dissent that determines whether bad decisions get corrected or entrenched.
insights.locator: Who Speaks Truth to Power?

insights.claim: Announcing a pause on a rewrite as 'We're not doing React' — a statement Gudeman says was not even true — caused one of the top front-end engineers to quit the next day, with no postmortem he is aware of.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Single sentences from executives carry measurable retention cost; communication precision is a real operational risk in talent-constrained teams.
insights.quote: the way it was communicated, because of the confusion, was, "We're not doing React". Well, one of the quality front engineers quit like the next day.
insights.locator: The "We're Not Doing React" Communication Failure

insights.claim: Gudeman frames recruiting leverage as three levers — salary, rocket-ship equity, and competitive tech stack plus developer quality of life — and notes that since most startups are cash-poor and unknown, developer experience is the cheap lever, so a team with none of the three is in trouble.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Explains why cash-poor startups over-invest in modern stacks: it is the only affordable recruiting lever, which drives real technology adoption cycles.
insights.quote: Salary, like in a rocket ship, then you can do equity. And then if you don't have those, well, you got to be competitive on tech stack and dev quality of life.
insights.locator: The "We're Not Doing React" Communication Failure

insights.claim: The company eventually migrated to React anyway after Gudeman left because the entire industry was moving to React, so the demoralising announcement bought nothing and cost talent.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Industry-wide stack gravity makes resisting a dominant framework a temporary and expensive delay, not a strategy.
insights.quote: They ended up migrating to React because it's impossible not to. The entire industry was moving to React.
insights.locator: The "We're Not Doing React" Communication Failure

insights.claim: Gudeman's prescription for executives is to never announce rejection of a specific technology and instead explain a course correction in terms of business focus, while explicitly acknowledging the parts of the domain outside your expertise.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A cheap operational fix with direct retention payoff — worth checking whether portfolio-company leaders practise it.
insights.locator: The "We're Not Doing React" Communication Failure

themes.theme: Career stage selection and equity realism

insights.claim: Gudeman advises engineers optimising for money, stability, structure and personal life to target big growing companies such as Meta or, if lucky, OpenAI, rather than startups.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Names which employers currently absorb talent optimising for stability — relevant to where scarce senior engineering supply flows.
insights.locator: Advice for Early- and Mid-Career Engineers

insights.claim: For engineers wanting startup exposure without extreme risk, Gudeman recommends post-Series B or Series C, or pre-IPO with IPO on the roadmap, because at that point there is usually product-market fit, a clear roadmap and priorities, acceptable compensation, and a lottery-ticket element.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A risk-adjusted staging heuristic that also predicts where growth-stage companies can and cannot compete for senior talent.
insights.locator: Advice for Early- and Mid-Career Engineers

insights.claim: Gudeman cites Figma as evidence that even a late-stage bet can fail for employees, saying friends who joined are in a rough spot with the stock price in the gutter.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A named case where post-IPO equity disappointed — relevant both to Figma sentiment and to how engineering talent now prices late-stage equity.
insights.quote: You could also be unlucky, as unfortunately we've seen with Figma. It's, I don't know, pretty rough. I have friends that went to work at Figma and stock price is in the gutter.
insights.locator: Advice for Early- and Mid-Career Engineers

insights.claim: Gudeman tells engineers joining seed or Series A startups not to expect the equity to be worth anything and that it is very likely not a wise financial decision — the return is the experience, the people, exposure to new fields and seeing how the sausage is made.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: A practising CTO publicly discounting early-stage equity to zero signals weakening recruiting leverage for seed companies relying on option upside.
insights.quote: I always tell people, "Don't really expect that equity to be worth anything". I really mean that. It can be someday maybe, but many times it won't be. You'll get zero.
insights.locator: Advice for Early- and Mid-Career Engineers

insights.claim: Gudeman characterises the early-stage appeal as wearing many hats and problem-solving across areas on the frontier, while simultaneously having little support and making decisions under limited resources, limited time and non-ideal conditions.
insights.speaker: David Gudeman
insights.so_what: Frames the actual compensation of early-stage work as optionality and skill acquisition, which is what founders must sell when cash and equity cannot compete.
insights.quote: it's kind of a double-edged sword
insights.locator: The Double-Edged Sword of Early-Stage Startups
